subject: On the appropriateness of the 1D- SPDE on time series problems

messages.author: 7a0c0a1d5af6ca55
messages.subject: On the appropriateness of the 1D- SPDE on time series problems
parts:
This is more of a conceptual question, not a software-related issue.

I have a question regarding the use of the 1D-SPDE with Matérn covariance for a time series problem. My data has two columns: time and y, where time is discrete (1, 2, 3, …), and for now, we can assume y is Gaussian.

I am familiar with AR/ARIMA/RW1/RW2 models, where the model fit references only past values i.e. Y(t) = b0 + b1*Y(t-1).

Does the SPDE approach handle this kind of time-dependence internally? For example, if I fix the range at 10 (so that observations within a distance of 10 have more influence on the current point), and I’m modeling at time t=40, I expect the model to mainly use observations from time 30 to 39 to influence the fit at time 40. However, since time points 41 to 50 are also within the distance of 10, does the SPDE model also use those future observations in the fit?

Do correct my thinking on the range if I got it wrong.

I hope this is clear. Thank you for your help!

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] On the appropriateness of the 1D- SPDE on time series problems
parts:
For 1D, the SPDE with alpha=1 is the continuous version of AR(1), and alpha=2 is like an AR(2) model. Since you have an observation model on top of this, the posterior distribution isn’t a Markov process anymore, but yes, the discrete time AR and continuous time 1st and 2nd order SPDEs will behave similarly to each other (except that the matern model with alpha=2 leads to a specific subset of AR(2) models).
This of course assumes that the temporal resolution used for the SPDE finite element construction has sufficient resolution (i,e, at most distance 1 between the mesh knots).
Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] On the appropriateness of the 1D- SPDE on time series problems
parts:
Hi Stanley,

yes, the range parameter controls the speed at which the correlation
function decays over time, just as the AR-parameter controls that same
thing. For AR(1), we can relate the correlation range R to the
AR-parameter a_1 by a relation of the form
a_1^R = fraction. E.g. with fraction = 1/10, R*log(a_1)=log(1/10) so
that R = log(1/10)/log(a_1) (assuming a_1 is positive, so that the
continuous time model exists), and R is the time-frame at which the
correlation goes down to 1/10.
For the continuous model, the correlation function is exp(-t/R) where
r is the time-lag, and exp(-t/R)=1/10 gives t = -R*log(1/10) as the
time-lag for which it reaches 1/10. So the R value isn't the same as
in the other relation, but the interpretation is similar; it's just
scaled by a constant.

One can parameterise the models to have exactly the same
interpretation: To find the continuous range parameter that gives the
same decay rate as the discrete model, consider
a_1^R = exp(-R/param)
Then
R*log(a_1) = -R/param
and
param = -1/log(a_1)
(Note: the spde models use a heuristic definition of "range" that
doesn't exactly match this)

For AR(2), it's a bit more involved, but the same principle applies.

As for how this is linked to _observed_ values, it's important to note
that your interpretation only strictly holds when the AR() process is
observed _exactly_. A soon as some noisy observation model is added,
the strict "observations at 30 to 39 influences the fit at time 40"
becomes a bit wobbly as the _observations_ from 30 through 39 don't
tell the whole story. As a rule of thumb, that reasoning works, but
the details sometimes matter.
And as for observations "in the future", yes, if they are supplied,
they will be used. The estimation work on the model&data _as a whole_,
i.e. it does _not_ do sequential estimation.

Finn
